A.explanation: Curve starts at origin and flattens as $V$ rises because heating of the filament increases resistance $R = V/I$.

B.explanation: Straight line through origin means constant $R$, which is ohmic behaviour and ignores heating of the filament.

C.explanation: $I$ cannot fall as $V$ is raised from zero; the curve also starts at maximum $I$ when $V = 0$, which is unphysical.

D.explanation: Increasing gradient means $I/V$ increasing so $R$ falling with temperature, opposite to a metal filament lamp.

hints: Look at the axes: $I$ on the vertical against $V$ on the horizontal, both starting at 0, so the gradient is $I/V = 1/R$.
Recall what happens in the filament as $V$ and $I$ grow: power $P = VI$ heats the metal and its resistance rises.
Ask whether $1/R$ should stay constant, increase or decrease with $V$, then check which curve bends that way.
walkthrough: Start from the given change: $V$ is raised slowly from zero, so the $I$-$V$ curve must start at $I = 0$ when $V = 0$.
At small $V$ the filament is cool, so resistance $R$ is low and a small increase in $V$ gives a relatively large increase in $I$.
As $V$ and $I$ increase, heating power $P = VI$ raises the filament temperature, and for a metal the resistivity and $R$ increase.
Since $R = V/I$, then $I = V/R$ grows more slowly than proportionally, so the ratio $I/V = 1/R$ falls.
On an $I$ against $V$ graph the gradient is $1/R$, so the gradient must decrease as $V$ increases and the curve bends toward the $V$-axis.
Only the curve that starts at the origin with decreasing gradient shows this behaviour. This is option A.
